Correcting the World Map: Harvard Examines the Shift from Mercator to Equal Earth

2026-10-06 Liz Mineo, Harvard Gazette world map, Mercator projection, Equal Earth projection, cartography, Africa, UN resolution, Harvard, map bias
Read the source article

Quick summary

Harvard Gazette examines the ongoing effort to correct centuries of cartographic bias, as the Equal Earth projection — developed in 2018 — shows Africa at its actual size, challenging the Mercator projection that has distorted global perceptions of continent sizes for over 400 years.

Key takeaways

  • The Mercator projection, created in 1569, distorts the relative size of continents, making Africa appear much smaller than it actually is
  • The Equal Earth projection, developed in 2018 by Tom Patterson, Bojan Šavrič, and Bernhard Jenny, shows Africa at its true size of 30.4 million square kilometers
  • Africa could contain the U.S., China, India, and most of Western Europe within its borders
  • The Mercator projection was originally intended for navigation, preserving accurate angles and directions for charting paths
  • Google Maps uses a modified version called the Web Mercator Projection
  • The UN General Assembly has endorsed the shift toward more accurate world map projections
  • Harvard's Pusey Library houses historic Mercator globes that illustrate the cartographic tradition being challenged
